title: Where the gap is closed, the remaining question is procurability rather than capability
content:
Flowable and Camunda arrived at the same place technically and diverge entirely on licence. Flowable Enterprise is sold on-premise by a Swiss vendor with a German office under ISO 27001, so a public buyer can simply buy it: dead end. Camunda offers an archived Apache-2.0 build with no security patches after October 2025 and a maintained build whose licence permits only non-production use, with a key that may not be circumvented: the wedge survives, relocated from auditability to procurement.

The same logic runs through the other verdicts. n8n's technical gap is real, and its licence adds a second, independent exclusion — not OSI-approved, so tenders requiring open source cannot count it. Odoo's audit is LGPL and default-on, which removes the wedge rather than creating one.

Where a capability exists in every product in a category, the discriminator moves to the terms on which it can be acquired. That is a different research question from the one the seven-question screen was built to answer, and it should be asked explicitly rather than discovered late.
description: Camunda and Flowable both filled the slot, but only one has a licence a sovereignty-constrained buyer cannot accept — which is what separates a wedge from a dead end.
